source: Camerer, Holzmeister et al. (2018) Social Sciences Replication Project - Replication report of Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011)
finding: A pre-registered, high-powered replication of the Google Stroop priming result (Sparrow Experiment 1) failed in both data rounds. Direction matched the original but size was near zero.
numbers: Original: N=46 reported (authors later said n=69), r=0.437, t(45)=3.26, p=.0021, RT 712 ms (SD 413) computer words vs 591 ms (SD 204) unrelated. Round 1 (N=104, 90% power for 75% of original effect): 547.59 vs 540.42 ms, diff 7.17 ms, t(103)=1.12, p=.265. Pooled rounds 1+2 (N=234, 90% power for 50% of original effect): 541.06 vs 538.17 ms, diff 2.89 ms, t(233)=0.76, p=.449. First-occurrence-only analysis: diff 3.25 ms, p=.606.
limits: Only Experiment 1 (priming of computer words) was replicated, not the where-versus-what recall experiments (Experiments 3 and 4). Original authors did not share materials; they objected afterwards to design details. Wharton lab sample, not Harvard.
agent_relevance: The only replicated piece of the 'Internet as transactive memory' claim is the priming step, and it did not hold. Do not use the Google-effects result as evidence for a pointer-memory design.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science 2010-2015, Nat Hum Behav 2:637
finding: Across 21 pre-registered replications (Sparrow 2011 among them) a significant same-direction effect appeared in 13 (62%). Replication effect sizes averaged about 50% of the originals. Peer prediction markets tracked which ones failed.
numbers: 13 of 21 (62%) replicated; 12 (57%) to 14 (67%) on complementary indicators; mean replication effect ~50% of original; sample sizes ~5x originals; estimated true-positive rate 67%, relative effect size of true positives 71%.
quote: We find a significant effect in the same direction as the original study for 13 (62%) studies
limits: The page opened gave the abstract and reference list; the per-study table is in the supplement. That Sparrow is a failure comes from the study's own replication report (d01), not from the abstract.
agent_relevance: Treat single-lab Science effects on 'cognitive offloading' as roughly half-sized at best. The same discount applies to small-N machine results.

source: Hesselmann & Gollo (2020) No conclusive evidence that difficult general knowledge questions cause a Google Stroop effect. PeerJ 8:e10325
finding: A second replication with a design closer to the original (addressing the original author's objections) also found no Google Stroop effect. Evidence favoured the null.
numbers: Sequential Bayes factor after N=89: BF01=5.07 for the null over the question-type x word-type interaction. Against the exact pattern in the original, BF0+=16.43. Hard-question blocks: 825 ms general vs 821 ms computer words. Easy: 830 vs 901 ms (SD 366/620).
limits: Priming step only. Authors say evidence is 'not conclusive' (moderate BF). Does not test whether people remember where rather than what.
agent_relevance: Two independent failures (d01, d03) leave the priming evidence weak. Lowers confidence in any design that assumes agents 'automatically think of the store when facts are missing'.

source: Gong & Yang (2024) Google effects on memory: a meta-analytical review of the media effects of intensive Internet search behavior. Front Public Health 12:1332030
finding: Random-effects meta-analysis of 22 studies (34 reports, 2011-2021). The pooled d is called 'moderate but significant' but the extracted text gives no single pooled number. The memory-specific subgroup includes zero.
numbers: 22 studies in PRISMA; individual d from -0.85 to 4.38. Subgroups: cognitive load d=0.73 (CI 0.22-1.24); behavioural phenotype 0.39 (0.16-0.61); cognitive self-esteem 0.91 (0.23-1.59); cognitive measurement (memory tasks) 0.56 (-0.15 to 1.28), CI includes zero; psychophysiology 1.01 (-0.12 to 2.13). Only moderator that explained heterogeneity: region, Q=6.20, p<.05 (13.18% of heterogeneity). Region effects: North America -1.04 (-1.88 to -0.20), Europe -1.11 (-2.32 to 0.10).
limits: Outcome is a grab-bag (internet addiction, self-esteem, load, memory). Not a test of 'remember where, not what'. Published studies only; funnel plot described as roughly symmetric but no trim-and-fill number. The text came from a two-column PDF, so the headline pooled d was not readable.
agent_relevance: Closes the question on the meta-analysis: there is no clean pooled effect for the pointer-versus-content claim. The memory-task subgroup is not significant.

source: Harris, Barnier, Sutton & Keil (2010) Couples as socially distributed cognitive systems (secondary description of Wegner et al. 1991 and Liang et al. 1995)
finding: Secondary description of the founding couple study: couples recalled more than stranger pairs only when they used their own division of responsibility. When the experimenter assigned categories, strangers recalled more than couples. The radio-assembly study is cited as the organisational-team case.
numbers: No counts reported in this source. Qualitative result only.
quote: Couples performed better than pairs of strangers, but only when they could use their own system
limits: Secondary source. The primary papers (Wegner et al. 1991, JPSP 61:923; Liang et al. 1995, PSPB 21:384) are paywalled and I could not open them, so no recall counts, SDs or F values.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema idea: an imposed structure can break a working division of labour. Warns against forcing a rigid roster of who-remembers-what on a system that already has one.

source: Wegner, Erber & Raymond (1991) Transactive memory in close relationships. JPSP 61:923-929 (search-result description)
finding: Design only: 118 individuals in dating relationships of at least 3 months; couples versus stranger pairs on a categorised word list, natural versus experimenter-assigned responsibility.
numbers: N=118 individuals (from a search-result summary). No means or tests obtained.
limits: Not opened. Publisher and author-site PDFs returned access denied (403). Exact recall counts remain unknown.
agent_relevance: Founding human numbers are still missing for this subfield.

source: Liang, Moreland & Argote (1995) Group versus individual training and group performance. PSPB 21:384-393 (search-result description)
finding: Design only: trainees learned to assemble a transistor radio in groups or alone; a week later all recalled the procedure and built a radio. Group-trained groups (same members) recalled more and built better radios; authors credit transactive memory (memory differentiation, task coordination, task credibility).
numbers: No means, SDs or effect sizes obtained. OpenAlex lists about 1,015 citations.
limits: Not opened. Full text not reachable. The control (individually trained members put in new groups) also mixes in familiarity with the group, which the authors address with a mediation analysis I could not read.
agent_relevance: Founding organisational result stays secondary-only. Number-based claims from it must be marked unread.

source: Hollingshead (1998) Retrieval processes in transactive memory systems (JPSP 74:659) and Communication, learning, and retrieval in transactive memory systems (JESP 34:423) - search-result descriptions
finding: JESP study: 88 heterosexual dating couples and stranger dyads learned words in six knowledge categories and recalled later. JPSP study: intimate couples recalled more when nonverbal or paralinguistic cues were available. Couples gain when rewarded for unique-word recall.
numbers: 88 couples in the JESP study. No means given in the sources opened.
limits: Not opened; summaries from a search tool. Exact figures unknown.
agent_relevance: Retrieval depends on communication cues, which suggests the lookup step (who to ask) matters as much as the store. Supports making lookup explicit in code.

source: Feng, Yang & Poria (2026) Sigma-Mem: An Online Reliability Memory for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
finding: A small learned memory that records each peer's past correctness (competence evidence) and how peers' errors relate (relationship evidence), updated from post-decision correctness feedback. Used for routing or weighted voting. It follows reliability shifts and beats unweighted agreement on unseen tasks.
numbers: Trained on 2,963 events (math, RAG, code). Five Qwen centre models. Counterfactual shift: Qwen3-0.6B accuracy 61.01% (CF@0) falls to 46.22% (CF@90) for the base model; with memory and relationship evidence 71.10% at CF@90. OOD (PIQA, MMLU, OpenBookQA, SciQ, BBH, SuperGLUE): memory improved the base in 27 of 30 cases; BBH Qwen3-4B 20.38% to 28.66%. M-Route and M-Vote about 60.7-61.0% overall for each centre model; paper states both beat majority voting and best fixed peer (table cells garbled in extraction, so exact margins were not read).
limits: Peers are three fixed small models with clearly different skills; correctness labels come from the benchmark. The memory has trained components, so this is not a hand-written directory. At CF@50 the memory steered the centre model toward the wrong peer in several models (e.g. Qwen3.5-9B 61.94% to 56.91% with 4 peers). Preprint, one group, no equal-token flat-store baseline.
agent_relevance: Nearest published test of a who-is-good-at-what store: updating a reliability table from outcomes beats equal weights when peers differ, and fails when feedback is misleading. Partly answers gap 1 and gap 7.

source: Feng et al. (2026) Sigma-Mem - feedback ablation and peer-count generalisation
finding: Reliability memory keeps improving as more feedback arrives, and it transfers to unseen peers, but it needs real feedback. With only 5% feedback it is about at the majority-vote level.
numbers: Feedback availability swept from 5% to 100%; centre Qwen3.5-4B OOD accuracy ranges roughly 59-61% (majority voting about 59.1-59.7%). With 4 unseen-peer pools, Qwen3.5-9B at CF@90 rose 61.04% to 67.97%; at CF@50 it fell 61.94% to 56.91%.
limits: Figure values read from a text extraction; differences of 1-2 points, three random feedback masks, no significance tests.
agent_relevance: A code-held directory must be fed ground-truth outcomes. Without a verifier it has nothing to learn from.

source: MetaCogAgent: A Metacognitive Multi-Agent LLM Framework with Self-Aware Task Delegation (2026) arXiv 2605.17292
finding: Agents keep a capability profile (historical success rate per skill dimension) and delegate low-confidence tasks to the best peer. This beat single agent, fixed routing, majority vote and AutoGen on the authors' own benchmark with fewer calls than voting.
numbers: MetaCog-Eval, 700 tasks, 3 GPT-4 agents. Accuracy: single agent 65.3, round-robin 61.8, random routing 63.5, skill-fixed 70.2, majority vote 77.1 (2,100 calls), AutoGen 73.7 (1,456 calls), MetaCogAgent 82.4 (1,382 calls; delegation precision 0.841, ECE 0.087 vs single agent 0.194). Hard tasks: 79.0 vs single 58.0.
limits: Benchmark built by the same authors; no variance or seeds; API calls are a coarse cost proxy, not tokens. The profile is mixed with verbalised confidence.
agent_relevance: Gives a lower-call comparison for a competence directory plus routing. Partly answers gap 1, but not at matched tokens and not independently.

source: MetaCogAgent (2026) - ablations
finding: Every part of the competence loop contributes. Profile learning from outcomes adds the least; self-assessment adds the most.
numbers: Full 82.4. Without self-assessment 75.6 (-6.8). Without adaptive delegation 77.3 (-5.1). Without boundary learning (static profiles) 79.2 (-3.2). Without cross-agent evaluation 78.9 (-3.5). Without verbalised confidence 78.1 (-4.3). Delegation threshold 0.5 best; 0.3 gives 78.1 and 0.7 gives 79.6.
limits: Single run per cell as far as reported. Authors' own benchmark.
agent_relevance: Updating a competence profile from outcomes is worth about 3 points, smaller than the gain from deciding when to ask for help at all.

source: Bertalanic & Fortuna (2026) The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate
finding: With small open models, homogeneous debate costs 2.1-3.4 times the tokens of isolated self-correction and reaches equal or lower accuracy. Failure modes: copying the majority, peers' reasoning breaking right answers, and the vote discarding correct answers already generated.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Ministral-3-8B; GSM-Hard and MMLU-Hard; 3+ rounds. Modal adoption up to 85.5%; vulnerability to peer rationales up to 70.0%; oracle gap up to 32.3 points; up to 28,631 tokens per problem. McNemar tests, uncorrected p; two Llama comparisons (p=.131, .155) not significant after Holm.
limits: 7-8B models only, homogeneous teams, no structured roles. Does not test summary compression (CoThinker) or information-asymmetric tasks (HiddenBench), where exchange is required.
agent_relevance: Matched-cost evidence against open-ended exchange when every agent holds the same information. Exchange is only worth its tokens when information is truly split. Partly answers gaps 4 and 6.

source: Can LLM Agents Really Debate? A Controlled Study of Multi-Agent Debate in Logical Reasoning (2025) arXiv 2511.07784
finding: On a logic puzzle with known answers, debate success is driven by the strongest member and by team diversity. Showing each other's confidence, debate order and extra depth give little. Majority pressure suppresses independent correction. Overturning a wrong majority is the move that raises accuracy most.
numbers: KnightKnaveSpy puzzle, 745 observations in the regression: confidence visible +0.025 (SE 0.015, not significant); order +0.002 (SE 0.017); number of agents +0.066 (SE 0.014, p<.001); initial smooth accuracy +0.600 (SE 0.100); chaos in initial answers -0.117 (SE 0.017). R2=0.29.
limits: One puzzle family; majority vote is the final decision rule; model mix chosen by authors.
agent_relevance: Showing confidence or credibility labels did little here. Bears on gap 7 (credibility cues) and gap 8 (the sign of dissent depends on whether a strong reasoner is present).

source: Phase Transition for Budgeted Multi-Agent Synergy (2026) arXiv 2601.17311
finding: A theory of when several agents beat the best single agent at the same total budget. Gains require the organisation exponent to exceed the single-agent compute exponent; lossy messages and shared errors can wash the signal out.
numbers: Closed-form budget thresholds; validated on synthetic simulations only (abstract and setup read).
limits: Theory and simulation, no real LLM runs in what I read. Binary tasks with majority aggregation.
agent_relevance: Gives a test form for gap 6: a matched-budget comparison is the right yardstick, and shared errors between copies of one model (high correlation) limit the gain.

source: Xiong et al. (2026) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior. ACL 2026 / arXiv 2505.16067
finding: Agents copy the output of the retrieved record whose input is most similar to the new task (experience-following). Storing everything lets errors spread; storing only strictly checked runs helps. This is a direct check of the 'store all trajectories' design.
numbers: Four agents, success or accuracy by memory policy. Fixed good memory: RegAgent 67.53, EHRAgent 16.75, AgentDriver 40.11, CIC-IoT 71.50. Add-all: 55.48, 13.05, 32.32, 59.90 (below fixed in all four). Strict human-checked addition: 70.95, 38.50, 51.00, 85.40. Coarse automatic judges in between (e.g. 63.18 to 67.35 on RegAgent).
limits: Not an ablation of near-duplicate removal; it varies which runs are admitted. The table was read from a text extraction with interleaved columns, so row and column assignment was checked by order, not by layout.
agent_relevance: Supports quality-gating a shared store (admit only verified runs) and warns that similarity retrieval makes agents copy. Partly answers gap 5 (independent group), but does not test code or math.

source: Wang et al. (2026) MemTrapBench: Benchmarking Cognitive Traps in LLM Memory Use. arXiv 2608.20202
finding: Even correct, relevant memories can anchor the model and hurt the current task. Across two model families and five memory frameworks every memory strategy fell below the no-memory setting; a prompt telling the model to avoid memory traps recovers some of it.
numbers: Best methods lose more than 10 points versus no memory. Task Boundary subset: trap memory 31.05% vs trap-free memory 94.39% vs no memory 92.29%. Trauma case: removing the abusive-feedback text moved average score 69.43% to 84.33%. AdaptiveMem prompt helps by up to 14.9 points (from a search summary; not re-derived).
limits: Traps are designed by the authors, so they show vulnerability, not typical frequency. Does not test answer-first-then-consult ordering.
agent_relevance: LLM-side evidence for anchoring on retrieved memory (gap 10). A design could let the agent attempt the problem before it reads memory, then compare. This ordering is untested here.

source: MERIT: When Does Memory Help? A Cost-Aware Evaluation of Long-Term Memory in Tool-Using LLM Agents (2026) arXiv 2609.05441
finding: Memory lifts dependent-task success from 0.00 to 0.55-1.00, but agents ignore a correctly retrieved fact about half the time, and implementation matters more than design. A hybrid store did worst under stale-record corruption.
numbers: 23,440 scored episodes; preregistered 3-model 3-seed grid. Updated-fact recall: embedding retrieval 0.30-0.95 across models (max seed gap 0.45); update-on-write stores 0.70-1.00. Ignore rate 0.45-0.53; agents act on a correct retrieved value only 55% of the time. Stale-memory harm +0.25 for the hybrid (Holm-adjusted p=.030, the only Holm-significant harm); contradiction and distractor corruption small and non-significant. Swapping memory implementation moves success by up to 60 points. Best condition gives 2.7-3.9x the marginal utility per dollar of full replay.
limits: Corruption sweeps beyond one domain left to future work; GPT-4.1 and Claude Haiku 4.5 plus a spot check, not the whole field.
agent_relevance: Gives a cost-controlled yardstick (utility per dollar). Source credibility was not tested; only staleness. Gap 7 stays open for wrong-source testing.

source: Memory manipulation in LLM-based agents for multiple-choice QA (2026) arXiv 2606.29030
finding: Inserting false memories before a clean multiple-choice question shifts answers away from the correct option. The paper reports baseline accuracy and an attack-success rate per backend.
numbers: Baseline accuracy across six benchmark settings: closed-source backends average 91.85% vs open-source 77.10%. Attack-shift numbers were not extracted.
limits: Only the baseline numbers were checked; the effect-size table was not read. Security framing, not a source-credibility test.
agent_relevance: A source-tag filter would have to catch deliberately false entries. Not tested here.

source: Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents (2026) arXiv 2607.20972
finding: Agents do not use a memory store on their own: zero memory operations in 114 turns even when pre-seeded with the needed facts. Harness-side deterministic injection delivered the facts every time.
numbers: 0 memory operations in 114 turns; injection delivered in every injection-equipped seeded run (n=3) with zero false alarms; 39% of in-session re-reads re-fetched content already paid for before compaction; ten facts held only in conversation vanished at the first summary and stayed absent in 106 of 108 forced compactions.
limits: One naturalistic coding task, n=3 seeded runs, one group. A design argument more than a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-held lookup that pushes the right memory to the model instead of hoping the model asks. Bears on gap 1 as the delivery half of a directory.

source: Li et al. (2026) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs (HiddenBench, ICML 2026, PMLR 306)
finding: The ICML version reports the same headline as the preprint. The structured protocol is only evaluated inside HiddenBench; no task outside the family is reported on the page.
numbers: 30.1% multi-agent under distributed information vs 80.7% single agent with full information, 65 tasks, 15 models.
limits: Only the proceedings page was read this time (abstract-level). Full-paper numbers were verified earlier in the critique step.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: no independent test of the exchange protocol on tasks built another way.

source: Annapureddy & Thamatani (2026) The Epistemics of Agent Memory: consolidation decisions in long-horizon LLM agents. arXiv 2609.33013
finding: Four-phase programme on deciding what to keep. A learned promotion policy raised task success under a token budget, and a three-gate anti-leakage protocol is offered. Production retrieval systems keep information but score zero on cross-level transfer.
numbers: +22.7% task success with 7x compression (per abstract); episodic-boundary learner oracle correlation 0.691 vs a 0.70 bar; quality score explains r2=0.43 of governance variance.
limits: Abstract read only. Authors' own benchmark (ConsolidationBench) with an oracle built by construction.
agent_relevance: Source for an anti-leakage gate when scoring memory gains, relevant to gap 5. Not an independent replication of MATM.
